newsitem.title: ZAIRE: At least 5,500 killed since November in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: At least 5,500 killed since November in east Zaire.

text.p: Aid workers say they have found at least 5,500 bodies around the eastern Zairean city of Goma, many of them Rwandan Hutu refugees believed to have been slaughtered by extremist Hutu militia and dumped in latrines.

Filippo Grandi, head of the Goma office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said late on Thursday the refugees were apparently killed in their camps last month by Hutu extremists attempting to prevent a mass return to Rwanda.
Zairean aid workers found an estimated 300 corpses in a pit latrine on Wednesday at Katale camp, home to more than 200,000 Rwandans until late October and 25 km (15 miles) north of Goma.

The aid workers from the Emergency Biodiversity Team agency, recovering and burying corpses from around Goma, which Zairean rebels seized in early November, said they had so far counted 5,500 bodies, including 1,100 Zaireans killed in the city.
"This has been a very bloody conflict, not a smooth transition. This land needs a lot of humanitarian reconstruction," said Grandi, who also acts as spokesman for the Zairean agency.
The Zairean team on Thursday carefully removed wooden slats from a communal pit latrine in the centre of Katale camp.
Around 20 smashed skulls and an assortment of human bones floated in faeces inside the stinking latrine, dug eight metres (26 feet) through volcanic rock.
Several of the corpses had their mouths drawn back in an expression of pain. A duck trapped in the pit was still alive.
The Zairean aid workers said the bodies had been in the pit for more than a month because of their state of decomposition.
They believed nearly 300 could be hidden beneath the surface on the basis of their experience of many similar sites but it was impossible to say exactly how many were there.
The team sprinkled lime on the surface of the pit and re-sealed it before moving to a site in another part of the camp where they had been told that more bodies could be found.
More than a million Hutu refugees poured into Goma in 1994, driven out of Rwanda by Tutsi rebels trying to end the genocide of their tribal minority by Hutu extremists.
Dumping bodies in latrines was a common practice during the genocide when Interahamwe Hutu militiamen used them to deal with enormous numbers of dead.

Since the fall of the camps last month the Zairean aid workers have found hundreds of corpses of refugees in latrines. The Interahamwe had waged a campaign of terror to prevent their Hutu kin from returning to Rwanda.
UNHCR international staff had already quit the Goma camps, before the killings are thought to have taken place, because of the deteriorating security situation.
More than 500,000 Rwandan refugees returned home from the Goma camps last month while thousands of others fled to the north and west to escape advancing rebel forces.
Most Zaireans in the team hunting for bodies said they were volunteers, working out of a sense of duty to their community.
"The reason why they keep finding more bodies is that they keep exploring new areas," a senior foreign aid official said.
He said the Zairean aid agency had uncovered little evidence of large scale killings since the fall of Goma to the rebels.
The U.S. State Department last week said it was concerned at reports of killings by the rebels and had received permission from a rebel leader to send in human rights investigators.
Refugee eyewitnesses say about 400 Rwandan Hutus were killed by rebels at Chimanga camp, 40 km (25 miles) southwest of the eastern Zairean town of Bukavu, in a massacre on November 17.
Villagers engaged in looting continue to uncover bodies burned alive in houses, left rotting in cars after ambushes and in fields and dumped at massacre sites, an aid official said.

Systematic attempts to count the dead have been limited to rebel-held Goma. Aid workers have yet to reach areas outside rebel control where they said Interahamwe were herding refugees away from the border.
